text:
Uncertainty is sparking through Ukrainian communities in Philadelphia and elsewhere with temporary immigration protections set to expire on Monday, driving doubt about the future of 101,000 people who gained safety in this country after the 2022 Russian invasion.

Thousands could be at risk in the Philadelphia region, both those who have been granted temporary protected status (TPS) and others still hoping to get it.

Some people already have left for other lands, spurred by the unpredictability over their ability to stay here. Others have nowhere to go, their homes in Ukraine destroyed, their cities under attack, and their lives here bound to keeping their children safe and fed.

“Everyone is extremely stressed,” said Iryna Mazur, the honorary consul of Ukraine to Philadelphia, who is also an immigration attorney.

By law, she and other immigration lawyers and organizations said, the lack of prior notice from the Trump administration has automatically triggered a six-month extension of TPS. But the administration has offered no statement or clarity around that. As of Saturday, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services continued to list the expiration date as Oct. 19.

Last month, as protection for an estimated 170,000 people from El Salvador was set to end on Sept. 9, the administration posted a last-minute alert ― saying an announcement would be made later, and until then Salvadorans here would retain TPS.

No subsequent announcement has been made. TPS for Sudan, which protects about 1,800 people, is also due to expire on Monday.

TPS for Ukraine, Mazur said, needs to be both extended and redesignated, the latter opening the program to newer arrivals. She has been talking to elected officials about ways Ukrainians can be protected, and how at the same time local employers can count on retaining the workers they have trained and depend on.

Asked about the future of TPS for Ukraine, the Department of Homeland Security provided a statement from USCIS spokesperson Zach Kahler, who said the agency “is actively processing discretionary re-parole cases, including those for Ukrainians, on a case-by-case basis as the law intends.”

“Under this administration, all aliens are undergoing intense screening and vetting to better protect the safety and security of the American people.”

Immigration parole is different from TPS. It is a discretionary permission under which the government can allow a noncitizen to enter or temporarily stay in the United States.

The American Immigration Council says that government decisions around TPS must be published in the Federal Register at least 60 days in advance of expiration. And that if that fails to occur, as in the case of Ukraine, the designation is automatically extended for at least six months.

The government has advised people to watch for updates on the USCIS website.

“There’s a lot of confusion,” said Mary Kalyna, a Ukrainian American activist in Philadelphia.

The Philadelphia region is home to one of the nation’s larger Ukrainian communities, tens of thousands strong, and became a key point of welcome and resettlement after the Russian invasion.

“These are our neighbors, employees, parents and children,” Andre Krug, president and CEO of the KleinLife social services agency, said in a statement. “They were welcomed into this country, they followed the rules, and they became part of our community. Now they are being left to wonder whether they will be allowed to work, support their families, or remain safely in the United States.”

KleinLife, with locations in Northeast Philadelphia and elsewhere, assisted about 2,000 Ukrainians displaced by the war, providing English instruction, employment assistance, transportation, mental health services, summer camp, and after-school programming, the agency said.

It is not only Ukrainians who will be hurt by the end of TPS, Krug said. A price will be paid by area companies that depend on Ukrainians’ skills and diligence.

“Employers invested in training them and now risk losing reliable workers — not because of anything the employees or businesses did wrong,” he said, “but because the federal government has not provided a clear path forward.”

When the war started, Philadelphia and its surrounding suburban counties were already home to about 15,000 Ukrainian immigrants and 52,000 people of Ukrainian ancestry, part of an ethnic connection that stands a million strong across the United States.

The 101,000 Ukrainians who live in the U.S. under TPS were joined by 240,000 welcomed under humanitarian parole through a now-paused Biden-era program, Uniting for Ukraine.

The Ukraine Immigration Task Force, a nonprofit that helps Ukrainians fleeing the war find refuge in the United States, posted on its website that TPS had been automatically extended for another six months, to April 19, 2027.

“By operation of law,” the group said, “if the secretary of DHS does not make a final decision on whether to extend, redesignate, or terminate a country’s TPS designation at least 60 days before it expires, the designation is automatically extended. … As of now, no further action is needed by current TPS beneficiaries.”

The task force did not immediately reply to a request for comment.

Since the start of the war, Philadelphia has been a center of pro-Ukraine activism and assistance. People here have shipped everything from medicine to sleeping bags to baby bottles to Ukraine to support the war effort and the civilians there.

The Russian flag was twice stolen from the Benjamin Franklin Parkway, as Ukrainian American activists demanded it be permanently removed from the boulevard’s iconic rows of banners. Local Ukrainian Americans unsuccessfully petitioned for Philadelphia to end its sister-city relationship with a Russian town, saying the tie lent legitimacy to a murderous Moscow regime.

Many Ukrainian Americans in the Philadelphia region were staggered as President Donald Trump tilted toward Russia, blaming Ukraine for a war that prompted the largest refugee crisis since World War II.

Meanwhile, the U.S. State Department has issued a Level 4 “Do Not Travel” advisory for Ukraine, its strongest, telling Americans not to go there for any reason.

The department warns of ongoing military operations, checkpoints by Russian forces, limited medical care, and unexploded ordnance.

Yet without an extension or redesignation of TPS, says Global Refuge, a Baltimore-based resettlement agency, Ukrainians living in the United States could be forced back into those conditions.

“Ending TPS now would put families at risk and destabilize the lives they have worked hard to rebuild,” the agency said Thursday.

TPS has been a mainstay of U.S. immigration and humanitarian policy for more than three decades ― and is fast disappearing under the Trump administration.

Created by Congress in 1990, TPS enables nationals of designated countries to live and work in the U.S. while their homelands grapple with war, environmental disaster, epidemics, or other extraordinary circumstances. TPS does not include a path to citizenship or permanent residency.

Trump and his allies say, however, that TPS has become a backdoor means of continuous residency, that “temporary” means temporary and people must go.

As of early 2025, about 1.3 million people from 17 designated countries were living in the United States under TPS, according to the American Immigration Council. Since then, the Trump administration has ended or announced its intention to end TPS for more than 1 million of them, including about 330,000 Haitians.

Today only four countries retain TPS ― El Salvador, Lebanon, Ukraine, and Sudan.

Human Rights Watch Warns France Against Deporting Afghan Refugees to Taliban-Controlled Afghanistan

——————————–

Human Rights Watch (HRW) has urged France not to forcibly return Afghan nationals to Afghanistan, warning that deportees could face arbitrary detention, persecution, torture and other serious human rights abuses under Taliban rule.

According to Afghanistan’s Shafaqna news agency, Fereshteh Abbasi, HRW’s Afghanistan researcher, criticized France’s decision to hold technical talks with Taliban authorities on the return of Afghan migrants without legal residency permits who are considered a public security risk. She warned that forced returns could violate the international principle of non-refoulement, which prohibits transferring people to countries where they face a real risk of persecution or torture.

France’s Foreign Ministry announced the talks despite the absence of formal diplomatic relations with the Taliban since the group regained power in August 2021. Similar deportation efforts have emerged elsewhere in Europe, including Germany and Austria, amid growing political pressure for stricter immigration controls.

Human Rights Watch called on French authorities to assess each case individually and ensure that no Afghan national is returned to circumstances that threaten their life, safety or fundamental rights. The organization stressed that immigration enforcement must comply with international human rights and refugee protection obligations.

text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A lawsuit filed Thursday challenges the Trump administration’s sprawling effort to collect and analyze Americans’ voter data, alleging the government has obtained voter files from at least 47 states and handled the data in a way that violates federal law.

The 42-page complaint filed in federal court in Washington, D.C., claims the Department of Homeland Security’s secretive probe of the voter data, including a policy to combine it with commercial datasets, disregards federal safeguards and flouts the privacy rights of millions of Americans.

The case, brought by the League of Women Voters, the Electronic Privacy Information Center and the League of United Latin American Citizens, is the latest in a torrent of legal challenges that have emerged in response to President Donald Trump’s crusade against noncitizen voting, a concern he views as a serious problem but which research shows is exceedingly rare.

The Trump administration has consistently sought to exert more power over elections, even as the Constitution grants that authority to states and, in some cases, Congress. Judges have consistently upheld states’ rights to decline to hand over their lists to the federal government.

DHS didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Thursday’s lawsuit alleges the Trump administration has obtained voter lists from 47 states, even as 30 states refused to turn them over to the administration. It calls for the court to declare the administration’s collection of voter data illegal, block the policy and order DHS to delete and stop using the voter information it already has collected.

The lawsuit comes less than three weeks before Election Day, as the administration has continued to escalate threats to states alleging they are not doing enough to remove noncitizens from their voter rolls.

title: Sentencing Immigrants - Race, Racism and the Law
description:
Abstract Excerpted From: Eric S. Fish, Sentencing Immigrants, 99 Southern California Law Review 291 (December 2025) (447 Footnotes) (Full Document).

text:
Abstract

Excerpted From: Eric S. Fish, Sentencing Immigrants, 99 Southern California Law Review 291 (December 2025) (447 Footnotes) (Full Document).

The most commonly charged federal felony is the crime of reentering the United States after deportation. On average twenty thousand people have been prosecuted for it per year since 2010, making unlawful reentry cases about one-third of the federal criminal caseload. And that number is about to dramatically increase. President Trump’s Department of Justice has announced a new policy of charging felony unlawful reentry in every available case, and it plans to reassign federal prosecutors working on drug and terrorism cases in order to prosecute more immigrants. Roughly 99% of the defendants in unlawful reentry cases are Latin American. The charge is, by definition, a nonviolent and victimless crime. It involves only entering or being found in the United States after a deportation. Yet defendants in these cases are systematically punished more harshly than comparable U.S. citizen defendants are in other cases. This happens in two ways.

First, the United States Sentencing Guidelines count reentry defendants’ criminal history against them twice. The Sentencing Guidelines are a complex set of rules that produce recommended sentences in federal criminal cases. While federal judges are not bound by the Guidelines, they follow the Guidelines about 90% of the time in unlawful reentry sentencings. In a standard criminal case, the Guidelines create a recommended sentence range by quantifying two variables: the defendant’s past convictions and facts about the current case. Past convictions create a “Criminal History Category” between one and six, while facts about the current crime create an “Offense Level” between one and forty-three. But in unlawful reentry cases, past convictions increase both the Criminal History Category and the Offense Level. Reentry defendants thus receive much larger sentence enhancements for their past crimes.

This double counting is worsened by another problem: the arbitrary way prior convictions are used to generate enhancements. The unlawful reentry guidelines make large swings in sentence length turn on obscure details of a person’s criminal history. This renders sentencing in these cases uniquely random and uncertain. Multiple years in prison turn on minutiae like the precise timing of a deportation order or probation violation, or whether a state uses a determinate or indeterminate sentencing system. People with similar criminal and immigration histories receive vastly different sentences based on such technical differences. And this problem is further compounded by the difficulty of finding and interpreting state conviction records. Figuring out the recommended sentence is like solving a high-stakes logic game. Defense lawyers are commonly unable to discern what length of sentence a defendant is looking at. And because the system pressures reentry defendants to plead guilty at the first opportunity, defendants often find out at sentencing that their punishment will be more severe than anticipated.

Second, undocumented immigrants serve a substantially larger portion of their sentences than do U.S. citizen defendants. The First Step Act, signed into law by President Trump in 2018, created a new system of “earned time” credits for federal prisoners. Under that law, a federal defendant who is willing to participate in anti-recidivism programs can get up to fifteen days off their prison sentence for every thirty days served. That means their time in prison can be reduced by up to one-third. In addition, defendants receive these credits even if they are not assigned to a program or no program is available. The only requirement is that they not refuse to participate. But deportable immigrants are prohibited from both participating in First Step Act programs and receiving custody reductions. This means that, by law, an undocumented prisoner will serve a significantly higher percentage of their sentence due to their immigration status.

To illustrate how this sentencing discrimination works in practice, consider two federal defendants: X and Y. Defendant X is charged with escaping from a federal prison, while defendant Y is charged with reentering the United States after deportation. Both X and Y have identical criminal histories: two prior felony convictions within the past fifteen years, each resulting in a two-year sentence. Under the Sentencing Guidelines, both X and Y will have a Criminal History Category of III due to the two prior felonies. Assuming that there are no aggravating or mitigating facts (like using physical violence or returning to custody voluntarily), X will have an Offense Level of thirteen for escaping from prison. Y will start with a lower Offense Level of eight for reentering the United States. But Y’s past convictions will also trigger enhancements of the Offense Level. If Y’s first deportation happened either before or after their two felony convictions, their total Offense Level will be sixteen. If their first deportation happened in between the two felony convictions, the Offense Level will be twenty-four. The Guidelines will recommend a sentence of eighteen to twenty-four months for X’s prison escape. And for Y’s reentry, they will recommend a sentence of either twenty-seven to thirty-three months or sixty-three to seventy-eight months (depending entirely on the timing of the first deportation). Unlawful reentry is the only federal crime for which criminal history is double counted like this. And once in prison, X will qualify for First Step Act programs that will let X spend up to one-third of their sentence out of custody or at a halfway house. Y, as a deported immigrant, cannot benefit from those programs.

As this example shows, these rules create two separate and unequal federal sentencing systems. Undocumented defendants, basically all of them Latin American, are treated more severely for their past crimes and are denied the lenient sentence reductions that U.S. citizens enjoy. And the enactment history of these policies reflects nativist animosity toward Latin American immigrants. The large recidivist enhancement for unlawful reentry was first created in 1991 with no study and little debate. It was enacted in response to Congress increasing the maximum sentence from two to fifteen years. That statutory change, in turn, was driven by racial panic in Florida over Haitian and Cuban refugees causing a supposed crime wave. The initial enhancement focused only on a small number of serious crimes, including murder and drug trafficking. But it evolved over time into a general enhancement for all past crimes. The First Step Act, in turn, was the first Trump Administration’s signature criminal justice reform initiative. Since the Trump Administration has been the most anti-immigration presidency in recent memory, it is not surprising that the law excludes deportable immigrants from its earned time credit system.

These sentencing rules explicitly discriminate against immigrants, and their history reflects racist and nativist antipathies. It might thus be logical to look to the Equal Protection Clause for a remedy, or to the federal statute mandating that the Sentencing Guidelines be “entirely neutral” as to race and national origin. But defendants trying to make such arguments have run into a problem--the Supreme Court’s antidiscrimination doctrines erect numerous obstacles to such equality claims. Federal laws that discriminate by immigration status are only subjected to “rational basis” review. While these sentencing rules overwhelmingly burden Latin American defendants, the Supreme Court has disallowed racial discrimination claims that rely on disparate impact. And the Court adopts a strong presumption that government action is not motivated by racial animus.

But sentencing is not like judicial review. In the discretionary sentencing context, the judge is the legally designated decisionmaker. They are not reviewing the work of an agency or legislature. Federal judges are empowered to disregard the Guidelines and sentence a defendant anywhere within the statutory range. The deference concerns that have hollowed out Equal Protection doctrine thus do not apply to discretionary sentencing decisions. In other contexts, scholars have identified circumstances in which executive branch agencies engage in “administrative constitutionalism”--incorporating constitutional norms into policy more robustly than formal legal doctrine requires. Judges should also embrace a version of administrative constitutionalism at sentencing. Here I call this ““sentencing constitutionalism.” Employing it, judges should reject sentencing rules that create racial and immigration-status-based hierarchies. And they should do so even if those rules would be upheld in the formal constitutional review context. Justice Kennedy gestured at something like this approach in Beckles v. United States. In that case, the Supreme Court held that constitutional vagueness challenges do not apply to the Federal Sentencing Guidelines because they are advisory. But Justice Kennedy wrote a concurrence arguing that quasi-constitutional vagueness arguments still have a place in the discretionary sentencing context. Sentencing constitutionalism is also analogous to the idea of “imperfect” defenses in criminal cases. There are contexts in which a defendant cannot legally argue a defense like duress or self-defense, but the moral justification underlying that defense still clearly applies. Judges will often reduce defendants’ sentences due to such imperfect defenses. Sentencing constitutionalism operates the same way, but with constitutional equality claims in place of defenses.

Federal crack cocaine sentencing provides a powerful example of sentencing constitutionalism in practice, as well as a close analogue to the sentencing discrimination faced by immigrants. For sentencing purposes, the Guidelines initially treated one gram of crack cocaine the same as one hundred grams of powder cocaine. This caused crack cocaine traffickers to be punished much more harshly than powder cocaine traffickers for the same volume of basically equivalent drugs. And this had a clear disparate impact by race because crack cocaine defendants were almost entirely African American. Much like the policy of double-counting immigrants’ criminal history, these crack sentencing rules were designed without formal deliberation or policy analysis, and were made in response to a congressional statute enacted during a racialized moral panic over crime. The crack sentencing guidelines were ultimately upheld in direct constitutional challenges. But many federal judges have exercised their authority to disregard the crack guidelines and adopt less discriminatory sentencing practices. In doing so, these judges have adhered to a higher standard of antidiscrimination than formal doctrine requires. Judges should act similarly in the immigrant sentencing context. They should refuse to impose the discriminatory rules built into the Guidelines, and they should counteract the discrimination built into the First Step Act’s sentence reductions.

This Article has two goals: to describe how federal sentencing law discriminates against undocumented immigrants, and to propose a framework for judges to counteract that discrimination. It is organized into four Parts. Part I traces the history of federal immigrant sentencing over the last several decades, exploring how and why these unequal rules were adopted. Part II shows that these sentencing rules discriminate explicitly by immigration status, and in effect by race. Part III explains how the Guidelines’ double-enhancements for criminal history create a sentencing system where arbitrary details of a defendant’s criminal record dictate large (often multi-year) increases in their sentence. It also illustrates the problem with a real-life case. Part IV introduces the concept of sentencing constitutionalism. It argues that judges should exercise their inherent power over discretionary sentencing to counteract punishment rules that discriminate by race and immigration status. It also shows that federal judges have been doing precisely this in the context of crack cocaine sentences--varying downward to mitigate racial discrimination that has gone unredressed in formal legal challenges.

[ . . . ]

This Article has shown that federal sentencing laws explicitly discriminate against undocumented immigrants. The Sentencing Guidelines give them duplicative recidivism enhancements that do not apply to U.S. citizens. The First Step Act denies them sentence reductions that U.S. citizens receive. This discrimination contributes to a racial and nationality-based hierarchy in the federal criminal justice system. Undocumented immigrants, nearly all of them Latin American, prosecuted for entering the United States, are treated as a legal underclass. They are punished more severely for past crimes and granted less mercy for current rehabilitation. Fortunately, federal district judges can help counteract this discrimination. Sentencing judges have the power to disregard the Guidelines’ duplicative enhancements. They also have the power to correct for immigrants’ exclusion from in-custody sentence reduction programs. For nearly twenty years, judges have mitigated a similar injustice in crack cocaine cases by systematically lowering sentences. They have done so out of recognition that the sentences for crack cocaine are racially discriminatory, and that this discrimination has gone unremedied in ordinary litigation. Judges should do the same for undocumented immigrants.

Professor of Law, University of California at Davis.

title: Bishop: “We will not be silent” over ICE separations - Aleteia
description:
We will not be silent and the Church – that’s us – will accompany our vulnerable neighbors in concrete, sustained ways.
We will strive to be a loving presence in our society for our brothers and sisters.
Once again, the presence of ICE in our neighborhoods has caused considerable unrest, anxiety and even fear throughout the Central Valley.
Even if you have not been personally affected by the increased immigration enforcement in our region, many of those who sit alongside you in the pews have been affected, with some already having been detained.
We will not be silent and the Church – that’s us – will accompany our vulnerable neighbors in concrete, sustained ways.
text:
It breaks my heart to hear from some of my pastors that members of their congregations have been taken away abruptly and with little or no information coming from federal agents. Clearly then, many of those caught up in this recent immigration enforcement in our Valley are not strangers to us – they are family, neighbors and parishioners who are being uprooted from the lives they have built over many years among us.

We will not be silent and the Church – that’s us – will accompany our vulnerable neighbors in concrete, sustained ways. We will strive to be a loving presence in our society for our brothers and sisters. Our parishes will be present to them for healing and comfort. Accompaniment might take the shape of walking with families through long and complicated legal proceedings, showing up at immigration court, organizing transportation and childcare, and refusing to let anyone face this situation alone. We will speak up for them and will encourage one another to see this work of justice as a part of our baptismal call.

Even if you have not been personally affected by the increased immigration enforcement in our region, many of those who sit alongside you in the pews have been affected, with some already having been detained.

In recent days I have been in close contact with my brother priests along with our local interfaith and advocacy partners, to search out ways to help, comfort and accompany our people. It breaks my heart to hear from some of my pastors that members of their congregations have been taken away abruptly and with little or no information coming from federal agents. Clearly then, many of those caught up in this recent immigration enforcement in our Valley are not strangers to us – they are family, neighbors and parishioners who are being uprooted from the lives they have built over many years among us. Last November the Catholic Bishops of the United States forcefully pronounced that, “We oppose the indiscriminate mass deportation of people…and we are grieved when we meet parents who fear being detained when taking their children to school and when we try to console family members who have already been separated from their loved ones.” (Source: USCCB’s Special Statement on Immigration). These people are valued and beloved, they are part of the fabric of our community. It is frightening to them and disturbing to us that these current operations seem to have taken on an indiscriminate nature with little regard for the dignity of the human person.

We will not be silent and the Church – that’s us – will accompany our vulnerable neighbors in concrete, sustained ways. We will strive to be a loving presence in our society for our brothers and sisters. Our parishes will be present to them for healing and comfort. Accompaniment might take the shape of walking with families through long and complicated legal proceedings, showing up at immigration court, organizing transportation and childcare, and refusing to let anyone face this situation alone. We will speak up for them and will encourage one another to see this work of justice as a part of our baptismal call.

Brothers and sisters, we will advocate for real change and real reform. Our country and our elected officials must do better. We need tangible results that reflect meaningful and just immigration reform. Until such reform is achieved, the dignity of our immigrant brothers and sisters must remain in the forefront of whatever shape our efforts might take. In the midst of those efforts, to be sure, we are navigating in a chaotic and emotionally charged time. I encourage the faithful to pray for one another and to act out of a spirit of communion in all things, bridging divisions and treating one another peacefully and with compassion.

text:
U.S. citizens wrongfully arrested or detained by immigration authorities could receive at least $500,000 in damages under a new bill introduced in Congress.

Democratic Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández of New Mexico introduced the Justice for Citizens Wrongfully Detained by ICE Act on Thursday. Bonnie Watson Coleman, a New Jersey Democrat, is the only co-sponsor at the time of writing.

The legislation would establish a specific cause of action for U.S. citizens arrested or detained by immigration officers, or other law enforcement officers enforcing immigration laws, without a warrant or probable cause on or after January 20, 2025. Those citizens could bring a lawsuit in federal district court against the officer involved and the U.S.

Read More on News

If a court ruled in favor of the plaintiff, the bill would require an award of $500,000, plus another $100,000 for each day the person remained detained after the initial day of arrest or detention. Successful plaintiffs would also be entitled to reasonable attorney's fees and costs, as well as appropriate injunctive or declaratory relief.

The legislation would also prevent federal immigration agents and other law enforcement officers enforcing immigration laws from asserting absolute or qualified immunity as a defense against liability under the proposed bill. It would expressly waive the federal government's sovereign immunity for lawsuits brought under the measure.

Claims could be filed for up to five years after the cause of action accrued. Any award under the legislation would be in addition to any compensation a plaintiff was entitled to under another provision of law.

The proposal would also permanently rescind unobligated immigration enforcement funds made available under the One Big Beautiful Bill, Trump's flagship domestic policy.

Under current U.S. law, citizens who are wrongfully arrested or detained by immigration agents can sue in certain circumstances, but securing compensation can be difficult because of legal restrictions and immunity protections for federal officers. Existing law does not guarantee a minimum payout for unlawful detention. The proposed Justice for Citizens Wrongfully Detained by ICE Act would create a specific legal avenue for eligible U.S. citizens to seek damages.

Hundreds of U.S. citizens have been detained during the Trump administration’s hard-line mass deportation campaign. An investigation by ProPublica found 506 U.S. citizens detained by immigration agents since Trump returned to office.

"ICE does not get to trample on your rights and walk away without consequence. They cannot hide behind their masks and act like they have a license to break the Constitution," Congresswoman Leger Fernández said in a press release.

"My bill is about justice for those Americans and accountability for the officers and a government who violate Americans’ rights."

Detentions sparking concern

Newsweek has documented several cases of U.S. citizens being detained by immigration authorities, prompting concerns about racial profiling, enforcement practices and how agents determine who to stop or detain.

Dayanne Figueroa, a U.S. citizen and paralegal, said Border Patrol agents forcibly removed her from her car in Chicago. Footage appeared to contradict the government's account. Aliya Rahman, a U.S. citizen, said immigration officers pulled her from her vehicle and detained her while she was on her way to a medical appointment in Minneapolis. Brandon Siguenza, another U.S. citizen detained in Minneapolis, previously told Newsweek that federal agents tried to pressure him into providing information about undocumented immigrants while he was in custody.

Brian Garcia Morales, a Texas man who maintained he was a U.S. citizen, was deported to Mexico by ICE before returning to the United States after producing a birth record.

Several U.S. citizens have also been killed in shootings involving federal immigration agents during Trump’s second term. Renee Good and Alex Pretti were fatally shot by federal agents in Minneapolis during Operation Metro Surge. Ruben Ray Martinez, 23, was killed by a federal immigration agent in South Padre Island, Texas. Keith Porter Jr., 43, was fatally shot by an off-duty ICE officer outside his Los Angeles apartment complex on New Year’s Eve.

Democrats have introduced a string of anti-ICE bills aimed at curbing the agency's powers that have had little chance of passing under the current composition of Congress.

Leger Fernández's legislation was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee on October 15, but faces a difficult path through the Republican-controlled Congress. The November midterms could change which party controls the House and Senate, though the bill would have to become law before the 119th Congress ends or be introduced again in the next Congress.

title: Federal Court Confirms SNAP Protections for Green Card Holders Who Were Refugees or Asylees
description:
The court confirmed two important protections: Certain green card holders with previous humanitarian immigration status are exempt from SNAP’s standard five-year waiting period.
Instead, it confirms that qualifying green card holders with previous humanitarian status should not be subjected to the standard five-year waiting period.
The federal court ruling does not automatically extend the time you have to appeal an individual SNAP decision.
Because federal eligibility rules have changed recently, some public guidance may not reflect every update.
However, the ruling does not restore SNAP eligibility to every refugee or asylee, and other eligibility requirements still apply.
text:
If you have a green card and previously came to the United States as a refugee or asylee, a recent federal court ruling could make an important difference in your SNAP eligibility.

On September 17, 2026, a federal judge ruled that certain lawful permanent residents who previously held humanitarian immigration status do not have to wait five years to qualify for SNAP food benefits.

The ruling also blocked an unlawful federal deadline that could have exposed states to significant financial penalties.

But there’s an important distinction: This decision does not restore SNAP eligibility to every refugee or asylee. It specifically addresses protections for people who have become lawful permanent residents, also known as green card holders.

Here’s what changed, who may qualify, and what to do if you’ve been denied food assistance.

What Did the Federal Court Decide?

On September 17, 2026, U.S. District Judge Mustafa T. Kasubhai ruled in favor of a coalition of 22 states and Washington, D.C., in a lawsuit against the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA).

The case, New York v. Rollins, challenged federal guidance about SNAP eligibility and deadlines for states implementing changes to the program.

The court confirmed two important protections:

Certain green card holders with previous humanitarian immigration status are exempt from SNAP’s standard five-year waiting period.

States cannot be penalized under the unlawful implementation deadline established by the federal government.

The decision made permanent protections that had initially been established through a preliminary injunction in December 2025.

According to the Oregon Attorney General’s Office, the court ruled in favor of the states on every claim.

The ruling is significant, but it does not eliminate SNAP’s other eligibility requirements.

Who Does This SNAP Ruling Protect?

The decision is especially important for lawful permanent residents who previously held certain humanitarian immigration statuses.

You may be covered by the ruling if you:

Have a valid green card.

Previously entered the United States as a refugee.

Previously received asylum.

Previously held another qualifying humanitarian immigration status covered by the court’s decision.

The key requirement is that you have become a lawful permanent resident.

For qualifying individuals, the standard five-year waiting period does not apply simply because they recently received their green card.

That means someone who previously held refugee or asylee status may be able to qualify for SNAP without waiting five years after becoming a permanent resident.

However, eligibility is not automatic.

You must still meet applicable SNAP requirements, including income, household, and other program rules.

What About Refugees and Asylees Without Green Cards?

This is one of the most important details in the case.

In 2025, Congress passed legislation that significantly changed SNAP eligibility for certain noncitizens.

Section 10108 of the law commonly known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act restricted eligibility based on immigration status.

Under those changes, people who hold refugee, asylee, or certain other humanitarian statuses generally no longer qualify for SNAP based solely on those statuses.

However, individuals who later become lawful permanent residents may qualify under the rules that apply to green card holders.

The September 2026 court decision does not reverse the restrictions for refugees and asylees who have not obtained permanent resident status.

Instead, it confirms that qualifying green card holders with previous humanitarian status should not be subjected to the standard five-year waiting period.

Other exceptions and individual circumstances may affect eligibility, so it’s important to ask your state SNAP agency about your specific situation.

Why Was There Confusion About the Five-Year Waiting Period?

Many lawful permanent residents must generally wait five years before becoming eligible for SNAP, unless they qualify for an exception.

But certain humanitarian immigrants have special protections under federal law.

After the 2025 SNAP changes, USDA issued guidance that states argued incorrectly described the eligibility of people who had previously held refugee, asylee, or other humanitarian statuses.

The guidance created confusion about whether those individuals could receive SNAP after becoming permanent residents.

In particular, states argued that qualifying individuals should not be forced to complete a new five-year waiting period.

That distinction matters.

Someone who entered the country as a refugee and later obtained a green card should not necessarily be treated the same as another permanent resident who does not qualify for a humanitarian exception.

The states challenged USDA’s interpretation because they believed it could result in eligible families losing access to food assistance.

Didn’t USDA Already Correct Its Guidance?

Yes.

In December 2025, USDA issued additional clarification about SNAP eligibility for certain lawful permanent residents with humanitarian immigration backgrounds.

That clarification recognized that qualifying individuals could remain eligible without serving the standard five-year waiting period.

However, the legal dispute continued.

The states were also challenging the federal government’s implementation deadlines and the possibility of financial penalties connected to how they administered SNAP.

The September 2026 ruling addressed those remaining legal issues and confirmed the protections for qualifying permanent residents.

This means the court decision did not suddenly create an entirely new SNAP benefit.

Instead, it reinforced the legal interpretation that certain humanitarian immigrants who become permanent residents are exempt from the five-year waiting period.

Why Did the Court Block Federal Penalties Against States?

The lawsuit wasn’t only about individual SNAP eligibility.

It also involved how quickly states were expected to implement changes required by the 2025 federal legislation.

USDA had established an implementation timeline that states argued was unfair and unlawful.

According to the states, the deadline could have exposed them to hundreds of millions of dollars in potential penalties for errors made while implementing complicated new requirements.

The court found that the challenged deadline was unlawful and arbitrary.

As a result, the federal government cannot impose penalties based on that invalid deadline.

The decision also addressed the time states must be given to implement certain SNAP changes after receiving appropriate federal instructions.

These protections matter because state agencies are responsible for processing SNAP applications, determining eligibility, and administering benefits.

Clear implementation rules can help reduce confusion for both agencies and applicants.

Does the Ruling Apply Nationwide?

The lawsuit was brought by 22 states and Washington, D.C., and the court’s injunction specifically protects the participating jurisdictions.

The decision also explains how federal SNAP law applies to certain lawful permanent residents with humanitarian immigration histories.

However, families should not assume that every state agency has updated its procedures in exactly the same way.

The ruling does not guarantee that every SNAP application will be approved or that every immigration-related eligibility requirement has disappeared.

If you’re unsure how the decision affects your situation, contact your state SNAP agency and ask about the current rules for lawful permanent residents who previously held humanitarian immigration status.

What Should You Do If You Were Denied SNAP?

If you have a green card, previously held qualifying refugee or asylee status, and were denied SNAP because of a five-year waiting period, you may have options.

Explain that you’re a lawful permanent resident who previously held qualifying humanitarian immigration status.

Ask whether your eligibility was evaluated under the correct federal rules.

You can mention the September 17, 2026 decision in New York v. Rollins.

2. Gather Your Immigration Documents

If available, have documentation showing your current permanent resident status and your previous humanitarian immigration status.

These records may help the agency understand why the five-year waiting period should not apply to you.

Ask the agency which documents it needs rather than assuming you must provide every record.

3. Ask About a Fair Hearing

If your SNAP application was denied and you believe the decision was incorrect, you may be able to request a fair hearing.

A fair hearing allows you to challenge an agency’s eligibility decision.

Pay attention to the deadline listed on your denial notice. The federal court ruling does not automatically extend the time you have to appeal an individual SNAP decision.

If you’re having trouble getting your eligibility reviewed, a local legal aid organization may be able to help.

Legal aid programs sometimes assist with SNAP denials, public benefits appeals, and immigration-related eligibility questions.

You may be able to receive assistance at no cost, depending on the organization and your circumstances.

Can the Federal Government Appeal This Decision?

The September 17, 2026 ruling is a final judgment at the federal district court level.

That makes it different from the temporary injunction issued in December 2025.

However, a final district court judgment can still be challenged through the appeals process.

A higher court could potentially change how the ruling is applied.

For now, the decision confirms important protections for qualifying lawful permanent residents and blocks the challenged federal implementation deadline.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does this mean all immigrants can get SNAP without waiting five years?

No. The ruling concerns certain lawful permanent residents who previously held qualifying humanitarian immigration status.

Other immigrants may be subject to different eligibility restrictions or waiting periods.

Can someone with refugee or asylee status get SNAP without a green card?

Under the 2025 federal changes, refugee or asylee status alone generally no longer provides SNAP eligibility.

The September 2026 ruling does not restore eligibility based solely on those statuses.

Does having a green card guarantee SNAP benefits?

No. A green card may satisfy an immigration-related eligibility requirement, but applicants must still meet other applicable SNAP rules.

What if I was denied before the ruling?

You can contact your state SNAP agency and ask whether your case can be reviewed.

If you recently received a denial, check the deadline for requesting a fair hearing.

Where can I learn more about SNAP eligibility?

You can review official information from the USDA Food and Nutrition Service.

Because federal eligibility rules have changed recently, some public guidance may not reflect every update. If information appears inconsistent, ask your state agency for clarification.

Relief Recap

A federal judge has confirmed that certain green card holders who previously held refugee, asylee, or other qualifying humanitarian immigration status do not have to wait five years to qualify for SNAP.

The September 17, 2026 decision also blocked an unlawful federal implementation deadline that could have resulted in significant penalties for states.

However, the ruling does not restore SNAP eligibility to every refugee or asylee, and other eligibility requirements still apply.

If you have a green card and were denied SNAP because of a five-year waiting period, consider contacting your state agency to ask for a review.

By Tom Rivers, Editor Posted 17 October 2026 at 8:43 pm

Photos by Tom Rivers

ALBION – Betty Garcia Mathewson of Albion speaks during a protest today on Main Street in Albion focused on many local people being detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

The protest also was timed by nationwide “No Kings” rallies speaking out against executive overreach by President Donald Trump and an erosion of democratic principles and rights in the country.

Mathewson has long been an advocate for farmworkers. She said many of those workers in Orleans County recently have been detained by ICE.

“This is not the America I grew up in,” Mathewson told a crowd of about 30 people carrying signs. “All people deserve due process.”

Mathewson said the ICE arrests are disrupting families and dividing the country, falsely blaming immigrants for economic hardships.

“The people they are taking have been our neighbors for years,” she said.

Some of the protestors had signs against “No Kings” to highlight opposition to Trump’s authoritarian tendencies and expansion of executive powers.

Gary Kent holds a sign, “Democracy Dies In Silence.”

Many of the “No Kings” rallies urged people to use early voting in the upcoming midterm elections and try to empower a new Congress to rein in the president’s powers.

Trump has expanded ICE in his second term, with ICE officers more than doubling from about 10,000 when Trump’s second term started in January 2025 to over 22,000 now. The daily ICE detention population is up from about 40,000 at the start of Trump’s second term to about 70,000 people now.

The “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” signed in July 2025 infused tens of billions of dollars into immigration enforcement, authorizing an additional $45 billion specifically for detention through 2029.

Librada Paz of Brockport has been outspoken for many years about labor rights for farmworkers. In 2012, she received the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Award for her work to improve the lives and working conditions of farmworkers.

Paz said ICE has stepped up raids in Albion and the surrounding communities in the past two months. She said people are being picked up by ICE at the laundromat, while waiting at farm fields, and at their housing in the community.

She said they are often held at the federal detention facility in Batavia before being transfer much farther away, where it becomes more difficult to fight their cases legally because they are away from a support system.

“The citizens of Albion may not realize that a lot of people are being taken,” Paz said.

Betty Garcia Mathewson and her daughter Sienna stand near the intersection of Main Street and East Park Street to show their support for immigrants.

Garcia Mathewson said the country has long failed to update its immigration policies putting many people in vulnerable position even if they have no criminal record and years of contributing to the community.

She said many families are mixed with one spouse having legal standing to be in the country while others were kept out of the legal system.

“We are here telling the immigrants that there are people who care and are pissed off they are doing this to you,” she said about the ICE enforcement actions.

title: Hawaiʻi Lawmakers Press DOJ Over Honolulu Immigration Court Travel Burden - Hoodline
description:
Brian Schatz and Mazie Hirono and Reps. Ed Case and Jill Tokuda follows a Civil Beat investigation into a dramatic shift at Hawaiʻi's only immigration court.
The letter asks why longstanding virtual hearing practices were abruptly reversed and how the DOJ will prevent travel costs from resulting in removal orders.
Neighbor-island residents with immigration hearings were required to appear in person 87% of the time in July and August of this year, up from just under one-third during the same two months in 2025.
The GAO’s 2026 review of remote immigration hearings documents both the national figures and those tradeoffs.
Whether the DOJ will act on either request remains an open question tied directly to how the agency responds by its early-November deadline.
text:
Four members of Hawaiʻi's congressional delegation sent a letter Thursday demanding the Department of Justice explain why immigrants and their attorneys are now required to appear in person for Honolulu immigration court hearings far more often than they used to, and what the agency plans to do to keep travel costs from triggering deportations. The letter lands as neighbor-island residents describe scrambling to catch pre-dawn flights just to make an 8:30 a.m. hearing.

The push from Sens. Brian Schatz and Mazie Hirono and Reps. Ed Case and Jill Tokuda follows a Civil Beat investigation into a dramatic shift at Hawaiʻi's only immigration court. According to Honolulu Civil Beat, the lawmakers cited reporting showing that new Trump-appointed judges now require immigrants and attorneys to appear in person four times as often as their predecessors did. The letter asks why longstanding virtual hearing practices were abruptly reversed and how the DOJ will prevent travel costs from resulting in removal orders.

The numbers behind that reporting are stark. Neighbor-island residents with immigration hearings were required to appear in person 87% of the time in July and August of this year, up from just under one-third during the same two months in 2025. People with out-of-state addresses saw an even steeper jump, from 14% appearing in person in mid-2025 to 82% a year later.

A Single Courtroom, An Island Chain Apart

Hawaiʻi's immigration court sits in Honolulu, meaning anyone living on Maui, Kauaʻi or Hawaiʻi Island must fly in — often covering their own airfare and, at times, their attorney's travel as well — just to sit in front of a judge. Morning hearings start at 8:30 a.m., but the earliest flight out of Maui departs at 6 a.m., leaving little room for delay or error.

Bettina Mok, executive director of the Legal Clinic, a Honolulu-based nonprofit serving immigrants, said the state's island-spread population creates travel challenges not just for hearings but for biometric checks and ICE check-ins too. In-person requirements, she said, make it harder for people to meet their immigration case obligations. The stakes of missing a hearing are severe: an in-absentia decision can trigger an almost automatic removal order.

Federal law makes an in-absentia removal order conditional: the government must show the person received required written hearing notice and that removability is established. The law allows a motion to reopen within 180 days when exceptional circumstances caused the absence, or at any time in specified situations such as lack of notice. Those remedies have defined legal limits, giving added significance to the delegation’s request for the number of in-absentia removal orders. Federal law sets out the conditions and reopening rules.

Rescinded Guidance Behind the Shift

The policy reversal traces back to a 2022 Biden-administration memorandum that directed the Executive Office for Immigration Review to approve appropriate remote-hearing requests, reflecting what the agency has long described as a standing practice of allowing hearings by video conference. That memorandum was rescinded during the early months of the second Trump administration, and the DOJ has since argued that the EOIR director lacks authority to instruct judges how to rule on remote-hearing motions.

The current EOIR practice manual allows immigration judges to hold hearings in person, by video or by telephone; telephone testimony in a merits hearing requires the respondent’s consent after notice of the right to appear in person or by video. At a respondent’s or attorney’s request, a judge may waive either person’s appearance at a specific hearing. The rules permit remote participation but do not create a blanket right to it, leaving individual rulings at the center of the dispute. EOIR’s hearing-format rules describe that discretion.

Leilani Stacy, immigrant rights staff attorney at the ACLU of Hawaiʻi, said a formal executive-branch directive limiting remote appearances could restrict access to justice. Her warning comes as the delegation's letter seeks any written guidance, training materials or informal direction discouraging video or telephone appearances, along with performance metrics or judicial expectations that could be shaping how judges decide remote-hearing motions.

Lawmakers Want Records and a Policy Reversal

Beyond explanations, the delegation is asking for hard data: remote-hearing motion counts broken out by who requested them, where they live and whether they're detained, plus counts of motions to transfer jurisdiction and in-absentia removal orders covering June through September of this year and the same stretch in 2025. The DOJ has been asked to respond by November 5.

The Honolulu dispute unfolds against a national system that uses both formats: EOIR data analyzed by the Government Accountability Office show that about 63% of nearly 6 million immigration hearings in fiscal years 2022 through 2025 were in person and 37% were remote. In interviews and observations at selected courts, judges and attorneys cited reduced travel costs and greater access to private lawyers as benefits of remote hearings, while also noting uneven judicial preferences and limits on language interpretation technology. The GAO’s 2026 review of remote immigration hearings documents both the national figures and those tradeoffs.

The lawmakers also proposed concrete fixes — monthly immigration hearings on Maui, Kauaʻi and Hawaiʻi Island, held by video or in person, and a return to the policy allowing remote participation whenever attendees would otherwise have to fly to Honolulu. Whether the DOJ will act on either request remains an open question tied directly to how the agency responds by its early-November deadline.

title: 'No Kings' protesters rally in Clovis as Trump praises ICE agents - ABC30 Fresno
description:
The rally marked the second consecutive weekend of No Kings demonstrations in the region.
Participants said they were concerned about the impact of immigration enforcement actions on local communities.
On Saturday, Trump held a rally in Kentucky, where he highlighted his administration's record on crime and praised ICE and Border Patrol agents.
Fresno County voters backed Trump in that election, marking the first time the county supported a Republican presidential candidate since 2004.
For protesters in the Central Valley, Saturday's rallies were also about civic engagement and public discussion ahead of the election.
text:
CLOVIS, Calif. (KFSN) -- Demonstrators gathered in Clovis on Saturday as part of the nationwide "No Kings" movement, protesting immigration enforcement policies and what organizers describe as an increase in sightings of Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers across the Central Valley.

The rally marked the second consecutive weekend of No Kings demonstrations in the region.

Last weekend, crowds gathered in Fresno and Kerman.

Protesters also assembled Saturday evening outside the Tower Theatre in Fresno for a second straight night.

"We're a community of immigrants. Of peace. I didn't think I'd have to be out here after the Vietnam War, you know? And here we are saying what you're doing is not right and we don't agree with it. And we elected you," protester Liz Smith said.

Participants said they were concerned about the impact of immigration enforcement actions on local communities.

"It's just a bunch of hard-working people that are being affected. Just our neighbors, everyday people that we should love and really just help them out. They're people just like us," protester David Alvarez said.

The demonstrations came as President Donald Trump continued campaigning with 17 days remaining until Election Day.

On Saturday, Trump held a rally in Kentucky, where he highlighted his administration's record on crime and praised ICE and Border Patrol agents.

During the event, a protester interrupted Trump's remarks. The president repeated his claim that protesters are paid to attend his rallies.

"They get paid. We have them all over the place. They stand up, they say something, they get 250. It's disgraceful," Trump said.

Immigration enforcement has remained a central issue in Trump's campaign.

During the 2024 presidential race, he pledged what he described as the largest deportation operation in American history.

Fresno County voters backed Trump in that election, marking the first time the county supported a Republican presidential candidate since 2004.

For protesters in the Central Valley, Saturday's rallies were also about civic engagement and public discussion ahead of the election.

"Basically the expression of the First Amendment. Hopefully you can get some issues across, change people's minds about certain things. It just starts with that conversation, open discussion," Alvarez said.

The demonstrations in Clovis and Fresno were part of broader No Kings protests held across the country, with participants taking aim at immigration enforcement policies while the president continued a campaign schedule that included multiple rallies in the final weeks before Election Day.

text:
1 October was supposed to be the “deadline” for foreign migrants in Tripoli. In the weeks leading up to it, dozens of groups and pages on social media urged Libyans to take to the streets in openly xenophobic protests.

Featuring racist slurs and depictions of Sub-Saharan, Arab and Asian migrants, the widely shared Facebook posts were intimidating.

The migrant rights group Refugees in Libya even reported receiving a handwritten threat targeting “black people”, delivered with a bullet, days before the planned protest.

Eventually, the demonstrations barely materialised, overshadowed by a large teachers’ strike over unpaid salaries directed at Abdul Hamid Dbeibah, head of the Government of National Unity (GNU), which rules the west of the divided country.

Still, dozens of protesters took to the streets in Tripoli on 2 and 9 October, rallying in Martyrs’ Square and chanting “Libya for Libyans” and “No to resettlement”.

Similar demonstrations have taken place several times a month in central Tripoli since April, steadily fuelling hostility towards migrants.

With nearly 700,000 Sub-Saharan Africans living in the Tripoli area, including some 335,000 Sudanese refugees fleeing the war, the Libyan capital has become a major hub for migrants seeking to reach Europe.

Between January and August, Libya was the departure point for around 80 percent of the 19,000 migrants who reached Italy through the Mediterranean. More than 90 percent of departures occurred from western Libya, particularly the coastline between Tripoli and Zuwara, long known as a major launch point for boats.

Attacks on migrant aid agencies

Already exposed to smuggling networks, arbitrary detention, kidnapping, torture and slavery – “systematic human rights violations and abuses”, according to the UN – as well as violent interception at sea, migrants now face growing threats in their homes and workplaces.

“I feel that Libyans are increasingly allowed to do whatever they want to us, without obligation to abide by the law,” Albert G, a 37-year-old Sierra Leonean living in eastern Tripoli, told Middle East Eye.

“Not only will torture and imprisonment continue to be a reality for migrants, which is already a well-known problem, but it also adds more common difficulties when there is no way for us to enter the public places or look for work to survive.”

‘I feel that Libyans are increasingly allowed to do whatever they want to us, without obligation to abide by the law’

– Albert, Sierra Leonean migrant

Albert says hostility began rising with the first protests in spring and became genuinely frightening at the start of summer.

In June, large crowds of Libyans protested for the first time against what they called a “resettlement plan”, allegedly orchestrated by the United Nations to prevent migrants from leaving the country.

Despite firm denials from the International Organization for Migration (IOM) and the UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), hundreds of protesters blocked the UNHCR headquarters in Tripoli on 4 June, accusing international agencies of trying to alter Libya’s demographics.

The protests were accompanied by anti‑migrant violence and waves of arrests of Sub-Saharans by the police and armed factions aligned with the interior ministry across several western Libyan cities, prompting many Sub‑Saharan people to remain indoors for days.

Although the unrest subsided during the summer, small gatherings and sporadic incidents continued.

On 7 September, tensions escalated when a group of Libyans stormed an IOM Migrants' Response Centre in western Tripoli. No casualties were reported, but the attack deeply unsettled the Sub‑Saharan community.

“If the authorities can allow an IOM camp to be attacked, many lives will be impacted because there will be no safe place for migrants,” Albert said.

Authorities accused of ‘complacency’

Following the incident, the GNU stated that “the right to peaceful protest can never justify assault, vandalism or threats to life”, warning that perpetrators could face legal action.

Asked by MEE about steps taken since the attack, the interior ministry failed to respond.

Meanwhile, popular Facebook and X pages created in spring remain active, spreading hate speech and promoting calls for mobilisation. Groups such as “Libyan News – No to the Resettlement In Libya” (76,000 members) and “The Tripoli Activists Movement” (39,000 members) continue to share hateful content targeting migrants daily.

The degree of coordination behind the movement and its origin remain unclear. A BBC investigation in August found that the June protests were fuelled by online rumours.

On the ground, public figures such as lawyer Thuraya al-Tuwaibi and journalist Salma al‑Shaab have repeatedly led protests – which they call "peaceful" – reinforcing their momentum.

“These campaigns are still ongoing, even though they are based on false and misleading information,” Ahmed Hamza, a Libyan human rights activist, told MEE.

“The actions of those advocating for or coordinating this criminal movement constitute criminal acts punishable under the Libyan Penal Code,” he added.

Hamza pointed to “a state of complacency, complicity, and suspicious silence from the interior ministry and other authorities”.

Migrants echo this sentiment, saying that while the GNU allows them to live and work in Libya – and sometimes even employs them – it has never guaranteed their safety in Tripoli.

‘I have never felt safe in Libya’

Kingsley (pseudonym), a Cameroonian refugee who has lived in Tripoli for four years, told MEE he has “never felt safe in Libya”.

Arrested twice by security forces in 2024 and 2025, the young man says he was released only after paying money to what he describes as his “kidnappers”. Beyond criminal gangs, armed groups affiliated with state institutions have been repeatedly accused of holding civilians to ransom.

“Now, I see the vast majority of Libyans as a threat,” Kingsley said.

‘Now, I see the vast majority of Libyans as a threat’

– Kingsley, Cameroonian refugee

While Sub‑Saharan Africans remain the main targets of online hate campaigns, some posts also target Palestinian, Syrian and Bangladeshi communities – particularly present in eastern Libya but increasingly visible in Tripoli.

Migrants also report more frequent violations of their rights and disrespect from locals amid the hostile climate, even when incidents are not directly linked to the anti‑resettlement movement.

“Last week, I worked at a construction site for two days and received no money. I had to go home on an empty stomach,” Albert said.

New protest dates have not been announced yet, but tensions around the anti‑resettlement movement continue to simmer, raising concerns that the situation could worsen.

“Authorities must assume their responsibilities. Matters could escalate and get out of control,” Hamza warned.

So far, the hostile climate has not prompted large numbers of migrants to leave Tripoli, but some are considering it. The IOM operates voluntary return programmes that assisted around 16,000 migrants in 2025, while the Libyan authorities deported more than 37,000 last year.
